impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, reinstating a jury verdict that found Eli Lilly willfully infringed. This case involves the blockbuster migraine drug market and directly impacts patent protection for biologic antibody therapies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain broad claims covering classes of antibodies where the specification discloses methods of making and humanizing such antibodies, even if only one specific antibody is exemplified.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face greater risk that broad antibody patent claims will be upheld, potentially delaying market entry for competing biologics.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2' to 'C1' in a chemical substituent definition between a provisional and non-provisional patent application constituted an obvious typographical error that preserved the patent's priority date, or whether it added new matter causing the patent to lose priority and be anticipated by an intervening disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment that Enanta's patent covering compounds used to treat coronavirus was invalid as anticipated, holding that Enanta could not claim priority from its provisional application because the change from C2 to C1 alkyl was not an obvious typographical error. Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid's active ingredient) thus anticipated the claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects companies like Pfizer from infringement claims where a competitor's patent loses its priority date due to discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional filings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent applicants face heightened risk that even minor apparent errors in provisional applications can result in loss of priority and invalidation of issued patents, emphasizing the critical importance of precision in provisional filings.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software trade secrets.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. It also reversed the district court's reduction of the breach of contract jury award, reinstating the original verdict. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirms robust protection for software trade secrets under both federal and state law, and preserves jury awards on breach of contract claims, supporting companies that license proprietary software.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal alternatives to licensed software face significant trade secret misappropriation liability, and courts may allow broader damages models on remand.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before the plaintiff brought suit, where the plaintiff allegedly had knowledge of misappropriation more than three years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's judgment and jury verdict in favor of Insulet on its DTSA trade secret misappropriation claim against EOFlow, holding that Insulet was entitled to JMOL because the statute of limitations had expired. The court found Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity on DTSA statute of limitations, protecting defendants from stale trade secret claims where the plaintiff had early knowledge of potential misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly once they become aware of potential misappropriation or risk losing their federal DTSA claims entirely, even where misappropriation is ongoing.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff presented legally sufficient evidence to establish that its asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret claims, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, holding that the same generally known ideas could not constitute an inventive contribution for inventorship. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens defendants' ability to challenge trade secret claims where the alleged secrets consist of generally known information, and clarifies the relationship between trade secret protectability and patent inventorship.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs must present clear evidence that their claimed secrets provide competitive advantage beyond generally known information, or risk reversal even after a favorable jury verdict.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar the defendant from asserting invalidity grounds that were not included in its prior IPR petition but that a skilled searcher reasonably could have discovered.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve on two invalidity grounds, finding that the lower court relied on insufficient evidence for one ground and failed to adequately account for hindsight bias for the other. The decision provides important guidance on the evidentiary standard for IPR estoppel in district court litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides accused infringers greater latitude to raise invalidity defenses in district court after IPR, requiring patent holders to meet a higher evidentiary standard to invoke estoppel.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders may find it more difficult to use IPR estoppel as a shield against invalidity challenges in district court, potentially prolonging and complicating patent litigation.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of a doctrine of equivalents theory for a multicore processor patent, and whether the court properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent asserted against Intel, finding genuine issues of material fact. The case addresses important questions about the territorial reach of U.S. patent law and doctrine of equivalents in the semiconductor industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against chip manufacturers gain clearer pathways to establish infringement despite extraterritoriality defenses, particularly for globally manufactured and distributed semiconductor products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor companies and other global manufacturers face increased exposure to U.S. patent infringement claims even where significant aspects of the accused process occur outside the United States.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury verdict form's use of a single question covering infringement for all asserted patents required vacatur, and whether certain patent claims directed to wireless building automation systems were patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding the verdict form's single question across all patents was prejudicially flawed. The court also remanded for further Alice step-two analysis on the '495 patent while affirming eligibility of the '887 and '371 patents' claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement for patent-specific verdict forms, preventing lumped-together infringement findings that obscure which patents are actually infringed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face greater procedural burdens at trial and risk vacatur of favorable verdicts if verdict forms do not separately address each patent.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that has granted an exclusive license but retained the right to independently sue for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue third parties for infringement possess an exclusionary right sufficient to satisfy Article III standing requirements, even after granting an exclusive license.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license rights but retain litigation rights can bring infringement actions without joining the licensee, providing flexibility in patent monetization and enforcement strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers cannot as easily challenge standing based on the existence of an exclusive license, potentially facing suits from both licensors and licensees.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a weight-to-weight ratio claim limitation to refer to free-base forms rather than salt forms, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta, agreeing with the district court's claim construction. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, holding that the district court must require the patent holder to post a bond pending appeal.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmation of injunctive relief blocking generic entry, and the claim construction supports broader patent coverage for drug formulation patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers are blocked from market entry, and the bond requirement ruling means patent holders seeking preliminary injunctions must be prepared to post security, adding financial cost to enforcement.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for automated collection, processing, and sharing of farming data were patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's agricultural data collection patent claims were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated the district court's finding that the case was not exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorneys' fees. The decision impacts the patentability of precision agriculture and IoT technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent suits involving data collection and processing patents in the agricultural technology space can leverage this decision to challenge patent eligibility, potentially recovering fees.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech companies and IoT patent holders face increased difficulty in enforcing patents directed to automated data collection and processing, and the remand on exceptionality signals heightened fee-shifting risk.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify outside of personal knowledge for purposes of establishing the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether the on-sale bar requires that a prior art sale expressly disclose the device's internal functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) corporate representatives may testify beyond their personal knowledge and that the on-sale bar does not require express disclosure of a device's internal functionality at the time of sale.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can more readily establish the on-sale bar defense using corporate representative testimony about historical sales, even when original employees are unavailable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges, as sales of products embodying the claimed invention can invalidate patents regardless of whether internal functionality was publicly disclosed.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied motions for JMOL on non-infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims relating to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital broadcasting, while affirming eligibility for other claims. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages, preserving a willful infringement finding against LG Electronics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical improvements in communications standards retain eligibility for certain claim formulations, supporting enforcement against standards-implementing manufacturers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement exposure, and the partial vacatur creates uncertainty about which claim formulations survive § 101 challenges in the communications space.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination regarding a sensor-based logistics patent, and whether a non-party to underlying litigation may file an IPR petition on behalf of or in coordination with a party subject to the § 315(b) time bar.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination for FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings, while declining to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. The case raises significant questions about potential abuse of the IPR system through proxy petitioners.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners gain protection from potentially flawed obviousness determinations by the PTAB, and the case highlights concerns about proxy IPR petitions that could lead to future reforms.
impacts.negativeImplications: The court's refusal to address the proxy-petitioner issue leaves open the possibility that entities not subject to the § 315(b) time bar may file IPR petitions challenging patents asserted in litigation against others.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents should be measured at a standard temperature of 25°C, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement by equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents by Mylan's generic drug, agreeing that 'pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at 25°C (the field standard). The court also upheld the ruling barring Actelion's doctrine of equivalents theory.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from this narrow construction of pH-related claim limitations, facilitating design-around strategies for formulation patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies with formulation patents face narrower claim scope when technical terms are interpreted according to standard measurement conditions, potentially reducing patent protection.
